utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's continue where we left off yesterday. I was asking you about the goals. Tell me, please: Who approved the bombing of the central television station, central studios of Radio Television Serbia? Because, as you know, it was a completely civilian target; there was no military in the building at all.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with regard to your last point, Mr. Milosevic, there are some doubts whether it was a completely civilian target, as you intimated. Some people believe that it was also used for communication purposes. The bombing of the TV tower was eventually approved by the Secretary-General of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here, in this statement, which this institution has prepared and which is called "Final Report," submitted to the Prosecution for a team set up to look into the bombing campaign of NATO into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, is that the representatives of NATO in Brussels told Amnesty International that they did not issue any concrete warning because that would jeopardise the pilots. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean with "any concrete warning"? To whom? Warning to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Concrete warning, which was otherwise envisaged that a warning be issued, according to Article 57 of the Second Protocol of the Geneva Conventions, when you are targeting a target of that nature. And it says here in the Prosecution document, the material supplied by the Prosecution, that you said in Brussels that you did not issue any concrete warning because that would jeopardise the pilot. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should have said this, Mr. Milosevic? Me? I should have said this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. It doesn't say any name here. It doesn't state anybody's name. All it says is the representatives of NATO, that they said that they didn't issue any specific concrete warning.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the issue of warning was discussed in the NATO council, that is correct, and it was said that we had issued a clear statement that we would attack targets throughout the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it was regarded as sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yes, that. But as it says here, and I was quoting it: Possibly the casualties among the civilians working in Radio Television Serbia are great because of the lack -- the fact that NATO didn't issue a warning. Now, as you are attacking the whole of Yugoslavia, then, by the same token, you consider that all the targets have in fact been announced. Is that what you want to say, having announced a general warning?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some extent, yes. But I also have to add, and you should note, that I was only there until the 6th of May. I do not know, and I never followed that in detail, since there was no longer any need for me to know that in detail and I had no access to classified information any longer, that some changes took place after the unfortunate event on the Chinese embassy on the 7th of May, and I'm not aware of the details of the discussion then. All I could say was what happened until the 6th of May, and there the policy clearly was that we should target targets of a military nature, and that was what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you've already mentioned the Chinese embassy, I should like to ask you to comment on just one paragraph. There is quite a lot about the Chinese Embassy here because allegedly you didn't know where the Chinese embassy was although hundreds of foreign diplomats attended receptions at that same Chinese embassy and knew full well where the building was located and so on and so forth. But let me quote here what it says under point 85 in the material that the Prosecution has provided me. "It is the commission's view that the crew of the plane that attacked -- launched the attack," and I'm talking about the Chinese embassy, "need not be ascribed any responsibility for the fact that they had been given the wrong target to attack. And also that it is unacceptable that higher officials be taken to task because the officials from other agencies got wrong information." Now, may you have your comments to that passage? Is this making fun of the Chinese and the truth at the same time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do I not want to duck your point, but I would like to remind you that I was no longer in NATO when this happened. So I'm -- I really do not know much more about this event of the Chinese embassy than what was published in the press. So I'm awfully sorry. I cannot give you any further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As we don't have much time, I would like to ask you a collective question. How do you explain the attacks on the convoys of Albanian refugees? How do you explain the targeting of the Dr. Dragisa Misovic hospital in Belgrade including the maternity ward of that particular hospital, the casualties that resulted on the -- from that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One question at a time, Mr. Milosevic. The first question concerned the attacks as alleged on the convoys of Albanian refugees. Can you assist as to that? No. You can't put a series of questions to a witness and expect him to answer. It's neither fair nor rational. Now, the first question related to the convoys.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it had been clearly stated by NATO that this was a tragic error, a pilot's error which happened, and I think no one regrets more than any of the military in NATO that something like this happened. It's one of those unfortunate events which happened in war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So that is your explanation, then. Now, tell me this: Who approved the use of cluster bombs, the cluster bombs that were thrown, as you know, throughout Kosovo on towns, including one of the largest towns in Serbia, Nis, in the central urban district of Nis which is where many citizens were wounded, especially children, by these cluster bombs. So who approved the use of cluster bombs, and who approved the use of the depleted uranium devices that were used?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Two questions. The first one, the cluster bombs. I'm not aware that cluster bombs were used against cities during the time that I was in the Military Committee. The use of cluster bombs against military targets was included in the approval of the air operation in general, and the final approval on the air operation was given by the NATO council. With regard to depleted uranium munitions, they were part of the equipment of the -- of an American aircraft which was used against tanks, and this ammunition belongs to the equipment of this aircraft. And since the aircraft was accepted in the order of battle, it was also part of the general approval of the air operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that include the fact that as you say that in the fight against tanks that they were not to be used in the bombing of urban centres such as Nis, the town I mentioned, in front of the hospital, the marketplace, the university building in Nis, and various other places?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if -- if there were no military targets hidden in these buildings or in these areas, then the munitions were not used against civilian targets. If someone used camouflage tactics to hide tanks, let's say, in a hospital surrounding, then the question is: Who violated international law first, those who took advantage of coverage protected by the International Red Cross in bringing military targets into the area of those protected areas or those who then attacked these military targets? I have to state in front of this Court, Your Honours, that I am not -- I do not recall a single event where NATO attacked a hospital. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You're not aware of that. That's an answer too. Now, you said that the exercises and training of our army in the winter of 1999 was allegedly a preparation for an action against the Kosovo Albanians. I'm now going to ask you, as a general, in view of the threats made by NATO from the middle of 1998 already and the intensification of those threats towards the end of 1998 and the beginning of 1999, was it logical to you that a country which is being threatened and on whose borders both towards Macedonia and towards Albania there is an amassment, build-up of NATO troops, that that country should undertake nothing with respect to the deployment of its forces in order to protect its own country?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the defence of a country and of your country in that case, I think, is absolutely legitimate. I would not -- I would not oppose such action being taken from a military point of view if one could clearly see that these exercises were meant to reinforce border protection troops. That, I think, was not as clearly evident as it -- as you just intimated. When we saw as troop movements in these winter exercises seemed to be a preparedness for forces outside Kosovo to deploy into Kosovo. Had the entire thing been done in such a way, Mr. Milosevic, that you had brought up to full wartime strength your 52nd Corps in Pristina and deployed it at the borders of Kosovo and then trained the reinforcement of those border elements, one could have seen a little bit more logic in that. But otherwise, since we did not know much more than what we learned from signal intelligence and satellite imagery, we came to the conclusion that you deployed forces in order to bring them into the Kosovo area, and with that you left ambiguous signals with us. One interpretation is the one you gave. The other one is that you prepared forces for actions against the civilian population in Kosovo. The only one who really knows it, Mr. Milosevic, is either you or the chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Answer me this, then, a professional question: As you mentioned the 3rd Army, within whose area of responsibility was the protection of borders towards Albania and Macedonia, as the 3rd Army, in view of the proclamation of a state of war, once you decided to attack Yugoslavia, and as it numbered over 150.000 men, what would you say the depth of deployment ought to be of an army numbering this many men, 150.000 men? Can they make a line along the border or must their in-depth deployment be over a large area? And as you know, the Kosovo area and the southern part of Serbia and generally that part of the country is not very big in order to be able to have a different pattern of deployment. So what would you say the depth of deployment and the area it covers ought to be for a strategic formation of that magnitude?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, I think you would definitely be right in what you presented in these statements a minute ago if there were not the fact that NATO had publicly ruled out the use of ground forces. I should say, from a military point of view, that was not the wisest of all decisions, but it was the decision that was taken. And you also saw, and your intelligence services saw, that there was no deployment of ground forces of NATO which really mattered in either Macedonia or in Albania. The small NATO elements which were there were part of the KVM protection force, and they were so small that there was no need for you to deploy anything but, let's say, a thin wheel of border-protecting forces, since your Pristina Corps, I think, outnumbered the NATO forces which were there in Macedonia and Albania by a large degree. So there was no need for you to deploy army elements, and for that reason I think all these preparations of the 3rd Army are, to some extent, at least, questionable. I cannot see a military justification for that, since no ground forces were there, and you knew exactly that NATO would need a couple of weeks to deploy ground forces in a sufficient number to launch a ground operation against Kosovo, which, by the way, as you know as well as I, is difficult to launch anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General Naumann, you're not really going to deny the fact that we had up in the area the threat looming with a ground force invasion as well?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is not correct. The threat of a ground invasion began to emerge with first signals after the Washington Summit, and from that moment on we tried - and I have no difficulties to tell the Court this - we tried to send signals to you which could indicate that a ground operation was about to happen. But before the Washington Summit, nothing like this was under consideration. It was repeatedly stated in public by NATO political leaders that no ground forces were envisaged, and on that ground, Mr. Milosevic, all preparations of the 3rd Army and of the 52nd Corps cannot be related to the defence of Kosovo and of Yugoslavia, since there was no threat of a ground invasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as you're talking about the 3rd Army, do you know that the 1st Army had been deployed because our side expected a possible ground invasion from the north as well? Do you think that we should have trusted and had confidence in what you were stating, what you were saying as to what you were going to do, or not, in a situation where there was bombing 24 hours around the clock? Why did we deploy the 1st Army, for example, towards the northern stretches?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not know what the threat assessment of your General Staff was, but the 1st Army, if I recall it properly, is in the northern part of Yugoslavia. If you deployed them outside of their garrisons, then it was a protective measure, presumably, to protect them against air attacks in the barracks. If you look at NATO forces in the north, you saw, and you may have noticed, that first of all there were no substantial NATO elements in the neighbouring country of Hungary and that the Hungarian armed forces were not in alert status. They were sitting in their garrisons and were doing peacetime training. So there was no reason at all to be afraid of a ground invasion from the north since no forces were there which could invade your country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You, therefore, consider that we, without any reason at all, counted with this possibility of a ground invasion. Now, you, as the Chief of General Staff of an army upon whom an aggression was launched, of a country an aggression was launched against, when you have the world's greatest power before you, would you have excluded the possibility, really, of a ground invasion and given up deploying your troops in readiness for that kind of invasion? As a general, would you have done that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, again I have to say I'm not aware of the risk assessments of your General Staff. I have always lived in my military life that I should take decisions to deploy forces only if I have a real reason to fear that something may happen in the concerned area. In the case of the northern part of your country, I think your General Staff would have really arrived at an assessment of the situation which is not based on facts if they believed that something could happen from the north without a preparation which may take four to six weeks or more, and there were no indications at all that forces were deployed to Hungary. And you also know from your political background that the country of Hungary has very strict rules with regard to the deployment of foreign forces on Hungarian territory. It requires an approval of the Hungarian parliament and the Hungarian president. Nothing like this was in the making. And all of this is in a democracy, done in the open, in the public, so your General Staff had, I think, every assurance that nothing could happen from the north without a warning time of six to eight weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That is customary that there are no war secrets and that everything is public. Now, you said that the plans for the deployment of these troops were probably prepared at least three or four months previously. Do you know that our army has plans, defence plans, plans for the country's defence, planned decades ahead, and that they are always updated, continuously or from time to time, depending on the risk assessment of the situation that prevails, and that every country does this; every country has ready made defence plans. They're not made once the country is actually threatened. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm aware of that, and I did not talk about plans of your General Staff to defend your country. I suggested that the operation, which obviously was prepared to act inside your country, and that is something which is different from the defence of the country, was obviously prepared well before the operation really started in March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that you consider that a country which has proclaimed a state of war, having been attacked and having become the victim of aggression, should not put into effect its measures and defence plan but should do something quite different regardless of how great the threat from outside is. That in fact it is not threatened from outside, it's just that it's -- hasn't got enough to busy itself with and has decided to undertake these measures to become occupied.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again I should say the only one who really knows the truth about all this is you, Mr. Milosevic, since you are the commander -- you were the Commander-in-Chief of the Yugoslav armed forces. We could only come to conclusions based on what we saw on the ground, what we heard by listening to your command channels, as far as we could do this, and whatever information we gained through intelligence. And based on that, we came to the conclusion that preparations were taken for military operations other than the defence of Kosovo, operations which obviously were partially aimed, at least, at the population of Kosovo and operations which were launched before NATO dropped its bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That, as you know, is not true, but I can't waste my time on that because my time is limited. Now, could you give me a brief answer if possible, please, to the following questions. My time is very limited. After the beginning of the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia, did you make statements for the public at NATO headquarters in Brussels on several occasions? That's a fact, isn't it? You did do so?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to give from time to time some statements in the press, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in those statements were figures such as 100, 500.000 allegedly killed Albanians mentioned?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five hundred thousand, you said? Five hundred thousand killed Albanians? I never said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which were the figures mentioned in your announcements to the effect that Albanians were being killed, hundreds of thousands of Albanians? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that I said on any occasion that hundreds of thousands of Albanians were killed. The figures which I mentioned were those which I mentioned yesterday in my testimony here, that more than --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying you personally but your spokesman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must make it plain. If you say "you" to the witness, he's bound to think that it refers to him. Do you know, General, of a spokesman saying anything of this sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I cannot recall that a NATO spokesman said -- spoke of one hundreds of thousands of killed Albanians. I'm not aware of any of those statements, and I can only assure the accused and Your Honours that in all the statements for which I had responsibility in the NATO council, we never used figures like this in order to indicate the magnitude of casualties or killed people of the population of Albania, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In point 35 of your statement that I have in front of me, paragraph 35, based on your interview with the investigator, you said that on the 25th of October, 1998, it was established that there were 10.000 in peacetime. Let me remind you. Ten thousand and twenty-four was the figure, and that is correct. There's no need to dispute that. But then in paragraph 35 you say that NATO had proof that the Yugoslavs had at least 500 excess police. First of all, that is not true. But even if it were and if the number of 10.000 was increased by 500 policemen, that is 5 per cent, which is statistically considered negligible. So a 5 per cent increase, is that a reason why we should constantly be threatened with airstrikes? Please give me a yes or no answer so we don't waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need to waste any time, Mr. Milosevic, since what I said in this statement is, I think, crystal clear. We discussed not the percentages and whether it is necessary to mention it or not. The fact was that we provided this figure to you in order to indicate that you were not in compliance with the agreement, that's all. And that was what we had as our intelligence at the time. Whether this was the truth or not is again a point which only you can reveal to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether this number could be a cause for such threats of bombardment regardless of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered. He has explained why the figure was given. It's nothing to do with airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We noted yesterday that you were aware that the KLA was abusing the October agreement because it engaged in all the activities that we referred to yesterday. So when you became aware that the KLA was abusing that agreement, why did you continue to threaten Yugoslavia when it was clear that it was the KLA that was engaging in these abuses?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I tried to explain this yesterday, and I said that many of the incidents were indeed triggered by the KLA, but your security forces reacted to these incidents with disproportionate force, and then they triggered the next step of escalation. So it's not a one-sided picture which you can portray here. It's both sides which were not behaving as they should, and you cannot one-sidedly accuse the KLA for being responsible for everything. There were also incidents which were triggered by your forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That question as to what is proportionate and what is disproportionate I hope is a relative issue. I hope we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this is an issue which one can simply put aside. I think you -- you will find a lot of sympathy if you defend your country against terrorist attacks, against subversive attacks with means which everyone regards as legitimate and proportionate. And I tried to explain this yesterday in front of this Court, and, Your Honours, I repeat it today. If they are terrorist incidents, I think it is the normal reaction of a country to defend itself by using the police forces. But it's disproportionate, at least in the view of the countries which I know, to use tanks and artillery to shell villages and cause casualties among the civilians and then go after the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That, Mr. Naumann, simply is not true, but let us go back to the agreement that you referred to yesterday or, rather, which the other party showed yesterday, and that is this piece of paper, single piece of paper, with a few lines on it. And it is true that this is my signature. There's absolutely no dispute over that. But one can see quite clearly, I hope, that I was not the signatory of the agreement. I accepted your request that by signing an agreement that you signed, Mr. Naumann and Mr. Clark together with Sainovic and General Djordjevic, because they were your partners, I confirmed that I approved such an agreement because that is what you requested of me. And you said to me, "Please confirm that you approve this agreement." And I said, "Okay. I'll put my signature on it as confirmation that I approve this agreement." So there's no mystery about it. But I do draw your attention to the following: Since this agreement was not really an agreement, it just says a record of a meeting indicating who was present. In the second it says that the aim of the meeting is to discuss specific steps. So the first item is a list of attendees. The second is to discuss specific steps that need to be taken for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to fully comply with the request contained in UN Resolution 1199. And the third item is the position of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the government of Serbia, which is presented in the attached announcement which the military representatives of NATO took note of, and you signed this. So this is a technical document, whereas the substance is contained in the announcement that this document refers to and which was not produced here, but it says, and I will just quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. You've been talking now for three minutes. It's time that we had a question. General, is the final comment correct, that this was merely a technical document and the substance was contained in an announcement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I understood Mr. Milosevic correctly, then he said that the first page, the page which has the signatures on it, is a technical document. And if he refers to this one page, then he is undoubtedly correct. This is a record of a meeting, and I would regard this as a technical document as well. But para 3 of this technical document speaks of an attached statement, and the attached statement is, with that word, I think an integral part of this entire document. And we had asked Mr. Milosevic also to take note and to authorise the actions which were contained in what is then called the statement. And as a matter of fact, I should again state that Mr. Milosevic obviously authorised the actions since we -- we saw the compliance of the Serb security forces with the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, is it clear to you that that is precisely what I am alleging?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, I think that was already discussed yesterday, and I stated in front of the Court that you were, for a couple of days, in compliance with the statement and that you also asked the withdrawal of the forces, as requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. But let me just remind you, because I was interrupted by Mr. May in my explanation, because as you yourself say, this was an integral part of this note. And it says, proceeding from the fact that organised terrorism in Kosmet has been defeated, that: "Since the 29th of September, 1998, no further operations are being undertaken against the terrorists. The authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia have decided, among other things, to take a series of measures which will contribute to the further confidence building among citizens, members of all national communities living in Kosmet, as well as to the resolution of all outstanding humanitarian problems, and especially the problem of the earliest possible return of all displaced persons to their homes. These measures are being taken with the clear objective to normalise life as soon as possible throughout Kosmet, ensuring security and well-being of all citizens and innocent civilians of Kosmet, and guaranteeing the rights of all citizens, members of all national communities inhabiting Kosovo and Metohija, to continue their everyday life without any restrictions, which complies freedom of movement of all citizens and representatives of state authorities, as well as the normal operation of all state bodies." And then it goes on to say that these forces should be reduced to the normal strength, that is, the strength prior to the outbreak of terrorist activities. And then it goes into the detail. So there's no dispute over that. And now I wish to draw your attention to paragraph III. I will not read it out in its entirety either, but it says, among other things, that: "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia calls on all other parties to unconditionally abide by Resolution 1199. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia will continue, by peaceful means and in cooperation with the OSCE, to find solutions to all outstanding problems." And then at the end it says: "However, the state authorities, as an extreme measure, and in accordance with the right to self-protection, retain the right adequately and proportionately to reply to all forms of terrorist activity and violations of the law threatening the lives and security of citizens and representatives of state bodies." Is that correct, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you just read out the statement which is in front of the Court, which is part of the evidence which this Court has, and I have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we did retain the right to respond to terrorism if it rears its head again, and that is precisely what we did when terrorism escalated, as it did, as you yourself stated. So is it not the legitimate right of a state to defend itself from terrorism?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I draw your attention, Mr. Milosevic, to two words which are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. included in this statement, and that is "adequately" and "proportionately," and that is obviously the point where we have a different point of view. No one challenges your right to defend your country. The question is whether you were in compliance with the obligation you took in this para III to respond adequately and proportionately, and there, as I have stated yesterday and repeat it today, I have every evidence that you were not in compliance with this obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the withdrawal of the army, as you yourself noted, created a vacuum, and the KLA filled in that vacuum, constantly killing civilians and members of the police and the army. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. I stated this yesterday. But there is also another side of the coin which has to be considered, and that is that your police forces took much more action than they were entitled to in the agreement on the police, since they increased mobile patrols and established, soon after the withdrawal of the excess police forces, additional checkpoints, which was monitored by the KDOM and by the KVM. So it's not only the KLA which took action; it is also to some extent your police, which was not in full compliance with this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't an increase of strength at checkpoints the result of the terrorist presence and, as we see from this document, in compliance with our right that we retain to react adequately in response to that? A checkpoint is no offensive unit or phenomenon; it's just a checkpoint, which needs to be strengthened if somebody shoots at it. Two policemen cannot man it and get killed. There need to be 10 or 15 to be able to defend themselves if a terrorist group appears. Isn't that logical, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If everything had happened in that way you just described, Mr. Milosevic, one could find a lot of sympathy for that point and it would be legitimate. But there was also -- there were actions where your police established checkpoints in areas where nothing had happened. They simply wanted to keep tight control of every movement of citizens, unarmed citizens, often absolutely innocent people who did nothing but peasants' work or things like this and were arrested by the police. So I think we would end in an endless discussion on who triggered which incident at which time. I think the fair statement is, as I said it yesterday and repeated it today: Many of these incidents were triggered by the KLA, but some of them were also caused by your police forces, and we saw an unfortunate tit for tat and an escalation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Naumann. Whether a checkpoint was placed were unarmed citizens were moving implies that you would know where the armed ones were moving around, but even the police couldn't know where the armed citizens were moving, and you certainly couldn't know, to be able to claim that the checkpoint was a place where unarmed citizens were passing through. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Milosevic. Of course we did not know where the armed civilians were and were the unarmed civilians were. What I just reflected was a statement of fact, that there were incidents where police people arrested peasants who were just doing their normal work on the fields, and there was no evidence at all of any terrorist attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us be as efficient as possible, please. Do you know that Zivorad Jovanovic, the then foreign minister of Yugoslavia, at the end of December 1998, addressed a letter to Kofi Annan, informing him that in the course of 1998, 1.854 terrorist attacks had been carried out in Kosovo, involving the death of 244 persons and the wounding of 566? Are you aware of this letter addressed to Kofi Annan containing these data linked to the UN resolution and all the efforts being invested and everything else? Quite impressive figures, I would say, of course in the negative sense. Just tell me whether you're aware of it or not, please. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of this letter, but you may forgive me that I don't recall the details at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that out of that, 470 terrorist attacks were carried out after the signing of the October agreement, together with 22 violations of the frontiers of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that may be correct. I do not know the precise figures. We monitored the events as good as we could. And the only thing which I would add as a comment is I would have hoped that Mr. Jovanovic had included in his letter as well the incidents in early spring 1998, which were not triggered by terrorist attacks, as you said, but which obviously were triggered by actions of your security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The early spring in Prekaz and Jasar, these were events that we have discussed here, and it is quite clear how many people were killed prior to that by them, so I won't dwell on that. Tell me, please: In your opinion, how many soldiers, policemen, and civilians did the KLA need to kill for the state to have the legitimate right to fight against it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think it would be -- it really would be ludicrous to establish a figure which triggers the right of a state to respond. A state has the right to respond to every violation of the internal order. The question is again and again, and there's a point where we really differ --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the proportionality or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You think Blair, in Ulster, in mid-1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Irrelevant. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The OSCE verifiers, or anyone else, did they inform you about the influx of weapons for the KLA from Albania?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OSCE informed NATO regularly on evidence they had, and as you may know, NATO considered actions to stop the flow of weapons through Albania into Yugoslavia, and some of these actions were indeed taken and were implemented with the consent of the government of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did NATO succeed in stopping the flow of weapons from Albania into Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you know better the conditions on the Balkan state. Ever in history anyone succeed in stopping all smuggling on the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely an exaggeration. But you will agree with me that NATO was not powerless to stop the inflow of weapons from Albania, and in that connection I have the following question: Paddy Ashdown stated here, sitting in your place, that he informed his government about this, which did nothing in that connection, and Klaus Kinkel, in August 1998, declared that Germany did nothing either to stop the flow of weapons for the KLA. So did you, I mean NATO - Clark, you, NATO - do something of substance to stop the flow of weapons from Albania?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think we did something of substance. We discussed all possible steps how to stop the flow of weapons. We proposed a couple of measures which the NATO council should consider. We were then not given the authority to stop -- to take measures to stop the flow of weapons there, where it all started, and that is there where the money is collected to get the weapon -- to get the money to buy the weapons. We were more or less given the task to stop the flow of weapons to the best of our ability at the final end, and this was the most difficult task, since we had only the means to stop the routes across the Adriatic and, to some extent, as far as the Albanian government gave us the opportunity, on the routes leading into Kosovo. And there we took some action. I think we achieved some partial successes, but we did not achieve 100 per cent success.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for stating that, that you were not allowed to stop it where it was possible to stop it. Do you know that the Helsinki Final Act explicitly authorises states to combat terrorism within its territory and that no other state has any right to prevent it from doing that or interfering? Please just tell me whether you're aware of that. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there we come back again to the old question. You state correctly what the Helsinki Final Act says, and I'm pleased to note that you refer to the Helsinki agreement. Also, you have chosen not to be part of the OSCE. And the other point which one I think has to consider is to which extent national sovereignty - and you refer to that by this statement - really means that a country can do inside its territory whatever it wishes to do to its citizens. I think that is an understanding of national sovereignty which emerged from the Westphalian peace in 1648, but it seems to me that the modern understanding of sovereignty means that the head of state has the responsibility to make sure that its citizens are protected, that they can live in freedom, and that human rights prevail. And that limits the acts of a state, in my view. But I think this legal question, this legal interpretation, may be considered by this Court at a different point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us not waste more time. You said that we chose not to be members of OSCE, whereas you know that we were illegally expelled from OSCE. The decision was taken by consensus minus one, though the rule is that such decisions should be taken by consensus. So we were expelled, and we, of course, protested. So how can you say that we chose not to be members of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this decision by the OSCE was triggered by your behaviour. So I think it goes back to what your country was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's just speed this up. Yesterday, we observed that the NATO intervention, the aggression against Yugoslavia, was contrary to the United Nations Charter. And I'm not going to go back to that now, but was the NATO aggression also contrary to your pact, the North Atlantic Alliance, in which it precisely states that it should not touch upon the system of security established by the United Nations Charter and that the decisive role should be played by the Security Council of the United Nations in that regard? So did you violate your own agreement and pact? And I quoted the point.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the NATO council took a decision based on the consent of all member countries in -- and the NATO council was fully aware of its own charter. It nevertheless came to the conclusion that the action was necessary and legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And Germany, according to its constitution, could it have undertaken operations outside its own territory?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any part of our constitution which bans Germany from taking military actions outside its own territory. We -- the only thing which is clearly banned in our constitution is the preparation of a war of aggression. That is clearly stated in Article 26 of the German constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the KLA burnt Serbs, Serb civilians, in the Klecka crematorium? Did you receive that piece of information amongst all the other information that you received about their operations? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least I do not recall it, and I think if some atrocity of that nature had happened, I think I would recall it. But I don't recall it, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why was it important for Clark and Solana to exclude terrorist units from the territory of Kosovo when it was clear that we were dealing with top-ranking terrorism in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please elaborate on that? I didn't understand what you're referring to since I'm not aware of that anyone excluded any -- any terrorist or something like that from Kosovo territory. Could you please explain to me what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not terrorists but anti-terrorist units, our anti-terrorist units in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we achieved an agreement that some additional special police units which you had deployed into Kosovo were to be withdrawn. And that is part of the 25 October agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You described three meetings. I don't want to repeat who attended the meetings, when they were held, et cetera, because all that was already quoted and I don't wish to waste time. But you did introduce a new factor, which at least for me, and I hope for the Yugoslav public as well, is very important, and that is the fact that your competent authorities in NATO took the decision to activate the famous activation order that you mentioned and that this was done at the request of Holbrooke. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is a very good thing that we should look at his two-faced role here, because he came allegedly to help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Stop the comments. If you have a question for the witness, ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you came to me for a meeting, I stated loud and clear that your information was not correct with respect to this overly strong use of force, and at the same time, we were conducting negotiations with Holbrooke. Isn't that right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Milosevic, that your negotiations with Mr. Holbrooke had come to an end, I think on the 13th of October. That is two days before I had the first opportunity to meet with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about - how shall I put this? - within the same time framework. And I said that NATO did not have the right to threaten to use force against a sovereign country; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You stated this when Mr. Solana came to see you on the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I told Holbrooke that too, and that was something that the press published as well, that the threats made to Yugoslavia were also -- also constituted a criminal act. And the press informed the population about that. So there was nothing covert or secret for this to be heard after three years.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not aware that there's any need for me to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's not a comment. Yes, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember very well that I told you and Clark, when you threatened that you would bomb us, that I told you, "Yes, you are a super power and you can bomb us, but then you will be war criminals." Do you remember me saying that to you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well, Mr. Milosevic, that you called us two potential war criminals, and I have also stated this when I was asked by the Prosecutor. So I'm glad that you confirmed that. We rejected this at the time, and we told you that we would act if ordered so on behalf of the NATO council, on behalf of 16 democratic countries who also tried to find a peaceful solution and to try to avoid hostilities, hoping that you would cooperate, but unfortunately, we failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, isn't it true that with this illegal aggression against Yugoslavia you in fact perpetrated war crimes, Mr. Naumann?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to answer that. It's just a comment by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I not tell you loud and clear that the army and police were not using excessive force and that they were acting completely within conformity of the laws of Serbia and Yugoslavia? Didn't I say that clearly to you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you stated this. I repeated that in my evidence which I gave to this Court. And we also mentioned to you that our view is different from what you call as legal actions. And again, we are returning to that like this famous cat which is walking on a pot of hot soup. It is again and again the question of the proportionality, and there is our basic disagreement. You regard, obviously, the use of tanks and artillery, and that has been repeatedly been reported by, I should say, neutral observers like the KVM observers, against villages of your own country, used by your own forces as legal and proportionate, and I disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you look through all the reports of the OSCE which were compiled at that time, during that period, and is what you're saying about our violations, does that emerge from those reports or was that some subsequent explanation, from some subsequent explanations fabricated later on? Because we received those Verification Mission reports too. Our side received them too, and you received them, as did everybody else. Now, are you basing what you're saying on those reports which were officially circulated by the Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base my statement on the reports which indicated that villages were shelled by artillery, were surrounded by tanks. And that was written in those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true -- is it true that I, in front of you, asked the chief of the General Staff whether your assertion was correct and that before your very eyes he said, "No, that is not what is happening"? Was that how it was or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He denied, that's correct. And that's also included in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When he -- you say that he perhaps had not been informed about that at the time. Do you consider that I could have been informed about the alleged incidents for which the chief of the army didn't know what was going on? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if the chief of the General Staff, Perisic, was not informed at the time, I also take it that you were not informed at the time, which doesn't rule out that the incident took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did I state to you loud and clear that the officials of NATO relied on unsubstantiated records by the KLA and that nothing that they said was correct and that I even suggested that your delegation hold technical reports with the -- negotiations and talks with the commanders of the police and army? Was that how it was, Mr. Naumann, or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I can assure you and you, Your Honours, that NATO never got any reports by the KLA. There was no information channel between NATO and the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what about contacts between Ambassador Hill and others? If they were not official, under the official cap of NATO, then I'm sure they do belong to the realm of information which NATO logically receives as well. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what ambassadors of individual NATO countries get as information I simply do not know. I do not rule out that Ambassador Hill may have got some information. You should also not forget, and you know that pretty well, that the KLA tried to inform the media on all incidents and that they gave their view of the picture as your people gave their view of the incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about -- that is to say, in point 17, para 17, and you devoted a lot of time to that, you say and claim that part of the conversation was focused on reducing tensions in the area around Malisevo and that the focus of attention on that day was Malisevo, in fact. Now, do you know what Malisevo was, that the KLA had its main headquarters in Malisevo, for example? And do you know why Malisevo was so important for your own side?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, with that you allege that we were taking sides with the KLA, which we did not do. And as I repeatedly stated, Your Honours, we did not have any contacts with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What -- Mr. Milosevic, what do you mean by "your own side" in relation to the general? Do you mean NATO? That's what one would take it to mean. Or do you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not insinuating anything and saying that General Naumann fought against the KLA, but -- on the side of the KLA. I'm sorry. But I do say that persistently and for a long time talks were conducted about Malisevo and that that is indicative because that is where the headquarters of the KLA were. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's suggested because there were talks which mentioned Malisevo, that shows that NATO, as I understand it, was in some way in contact with the KLA. Is there any possible comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Milosevic is talking about discussions in which he did not take part. These were the discussions which started in the -- in the General Staff headquarters. And what I stated was that based on the requests of the Yugoslav side, we started to negotiate on the situation around Malisevo in order to find an agreement there. And then we learned, after two or more hours, that we would not come to an end of finding a solution for the entire region of Kosovo if we continued in that way. So it was not us who started with Malisevo. It was the done on the request of the Yugoslav side. And it was obviously done since at the time when we came to Belgrade, Malisevo was the centre of tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The centre of what?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tensions. Yes. Now, I'm asking you now, General Naumann, whether at the time or perhaps later on it -- you became aware of and came to know that Malisevo was also one of the camps of Al Qaeda at that time.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware, Mr. Milosevic, that the word "Al Qaeda" was ever mentioned in any of the discussions I participated in on the Kosovo situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. May I just have your comments to several facts which I'm going to read out to you. Just a few of them. I have to save time, the time I have, so I'm going to be brief [In English] "[Previous translation continues] ...1994, major Balkan terrorist training camps included Zenica and Malisevo and Mitrovica in Kosovo. Number of Mujahedins operating before that time in Bosnia alone continued to grow from a few hundred to around 6.000 in 1995. So where was the US in all this? It was not until 1995 that Clinton Administration was forced to start pursuing the Islamic network in Balkans. Not quite a month after the Dayton Accord had been signed in November 1999, an influx of Iranian arms came into Bosnia with the apparent tacit approval of the administration in violation of US sanctions. Islamic infiltration --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's time -- it's time we came to a question. What you describe -- what you describe as facts are clearly some report which you have, which is the opinion, I suspect, of some journalist. Would you tell us what you are quoting from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you in just a moment, but may I finish? I have just a few lines to read out to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You will tell us now what it is you're reading from so we may understand it and then you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm reading from a report based on -- I'll tell you in just a moment. Based on information by Joseph Podansky, who was the Director of the US House of Representatives Task Force on Terrorism and Unconventional Warfare. And it was written by -- it was written by Christoph Corp, editor of the Washington-based weekly newspaper Defence News, Defence News. And it was published in its entirety by the Wall Street Journal in November -- on November the 1st, 2001. So there you have it, please. And may I read out just a few more lines which are remaining? [In English] "[Previous translation continues] ...of the Kosovo Liberation Army advanced meanwhile. Bin Laden is said to have visited Albania in 1996 and 1997, according to the murder trial testimony of an Algerian born French national Claude Kader, himself an Afghanistan-trained Mujahedin fronting at the Albania Agro-Islamic Bank. He recruited some Albanians to fight with the KLA in Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "[Previous translation continues] ...meanwhile, Albanian separatism in Kosovo and Metohija was formally characterised as a Jihad in October 1998 at an annual international Islamic conference in Pakistan. Nonetheless, the 25.000-strong KLA continued to receive official NATO-US arms and training support. And at the talks in Rambouillet, France, the Secretary of State, Madeleine Albright, shook hands with the `freedom fighter' Hashim Thaci a KLA leader. As this was taking place --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've had enough -- we've had enough reading. Now, the witness is here to give evidence, not you read out these documents. No. You're abusing the process again. Now, General, you've heard what's been read out. You may be able to see at least some of it on the screen while it's there. Can you help at all about this? First of all, do you know anything about this article, this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't seen this article. And I should also mention: As far as I saw Mr. Milosevic -- heard Mr. Milosevic read out, that the article was published in 2001, so I couldn't have been aware of the article at the time when the Kosovo conflict was all about. I'm not aware -- as I have stated, the word "Al Qaeda" was never mentioned in any of the Kosovo-related discussions I had with anyone. I should also add that I did not know, and it was never in any NATO intelligence, that Osama bin Laden allegedly had been in Albania. That is something I heard today the first time. So I think that is all what I can add to Mr. Milosevic's read-out. We knew -- but I take it that Bosnia is something which is going to be dealt separately in this Court proceedings. We knew that Islamic Mujahedin were in Bosnia. We took action with the NATO SFOR forces against some of these Mujahedin. But this has nothing to do, I believe, with Kosovo, and that's all I can contribute to Mr. Milosevic's read-out here in front of this Court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what I've read out, you can see that their presence was recorded from 1994 and 1995, let alone 1998, the supply of arms and so on. That's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has answered that question and says that they knew nothing about it, Mr. Milosevic, so it's really pointless going on. If it's true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when we bear this in mind, I'm asking the following question: Who is being told tales here about human rights? Isn't it quite clear that what is being attempted here is to help the former allies from this aborted Clinton Administration which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not going to ask that question. Now, you have theoretically half an hour more. Have you any other questions you want to ask which are proper questions and relevant? You raised the question of relevance before. By now you should know in this trial what is relevant and what isn't. That which is connected with the indictment is relevant, and that which isn't is irrelevant. Now, do you want to ask the general Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any more questions? You've exhausted this topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have many more questions, and since the witness is giving rather lengthy answers, I hope that you will increase the time that you say I have left, which is half an hour, because I do have a number of questions for which I would need a little more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, there will be no more time. Half an hour. At least, you've got five minutes more and then you've got half an hour after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you knew that young Serb policemen were being killed and tortured by the KLA and that incidents of this kind led to violence and counterviolence. That is what is stated in paragraph 8 of your statement. So you did have knowledge about that. Now, where do you get the idea from that a decision was made at the time to expel the Albanian population? Because you say -- let me explain and clarify my question. You speak about the fact that there was talk of national equilibrium. Now, haven't you mixed some concepts up? Because what was talked about was the equality of national communities, ethnic communities in Kosovo, and not the numerical balance and equilibrium thereof, because that is physically impossible. So are you aware of the fact that the key positions of our policy was the equality of citizens and the equality of ethnic communities, so that there was no majorisation, that national communities, ethnic communities, should be equal? Did you mix up equality with striking a balance when you speak about this balance and equilibrium?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, I did not mix it up. I remember very well that you repeatedly stated that you wished to see a solution in which all ethnicities and all nationalities in Kosovo would have the same rights. I think you did never live up to that claim in reality. And I remember also very well that you and Mr. Sainovic talked about the need that, in terms of quantity, a better balance should be there, and otherwise the same problem would return in a couple of years again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, better balance, Mr. Naumann. How can you strike a better balance either by expelling or killing? Is that the substance of your testimony, that by trying to justify the NATO aggression, you are accusing us of wanting to either kill or expel Albanians from Kosovo? How can the number be reduced otherwise but by expelling someone? And then you speak again of our political positions, which are quite contrary to that. Can't you see the contradictions in what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, I don't see the contradiction, since the facts speak against you. In spring 1999, I think hundreds of thousands -- at least a hundred thousand or so were expelled from Kosovo, and they were forced to leave the country, and this was done by your security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, in 1999, at the beginning of the year, I think that at least several hundred thousand Albanians lived in different cities of Europe, where they worked and where they had been living for a whole decade, et cetera, et cetera. So that is not something that is challenged, just as several hundred thousand Serbs have been living -- I don't know if they are tens of thousands in Vienna alone perhaps, or several tens of thousands in Paris, living in Paris, who have been working as guest workers throughout Europe for decades now. Hundreds of thousands of Albanians from Kosovo have for decades been living in Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Italy, and many other European countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're here to ask questions. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, how many of them there are outside Kosovo, that's not a question at all, it's not an issue, just as it isn't an issue how many Serbs there are outside Yugoslavia. There are a million Serbs in America alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we do not talk about those people who left Yugoslavia to be guest workers elsewhere. I referred to those people who were driven out of their homes in spring 1999 and were forced to leave the country, and entered, forced by your forces, Macedonia and Albania, where we established refugee camps to house them and to shelter them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time is now half past 10.00. It's time for an adjournment, and we'll adjourn for 20 minutes. Would you be back, please, at 10 minutes to 11.00, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraph 24, you said that I described the Kosovar Albanians as criminals, killers, and rapists. Is that how I called the Kosovar Albanians or the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, Mr. Milosevic, you referred with these words to the Kosovar Albanians who did not comply with your way of keeping them under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that I said to you that all Kosovar Albanians are criminals, murderers, and rapists; is that what you are claiming?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You left us with that impression. That's not only my impression; that's also the impression of General Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you and General Clark are claiming now, three years later, is quite transparent. But let me ask you: Since you mentioned Drenica, do you know that between the two world wars, in Drenica, there were bandits called Kacaks, and that the Royal Army had to intervene on several occasions because they plundered and murdered, in most cases, wealthy Albanians, as they were those who were the most numerous there? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, I'm not aware of that detail of the history of that part of former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the point, that Drenica could only have been mentioned as a cradle of terrorism and banditism, and in no other way, in view of these historical facts. Is that logical to you or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a question. The witness can only deal with what he saw and heard, which he has dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you declared that Clark wrote in his book that I said to you that I would find a solution in the spring of 1999 similar to the one in Drenica. But if you look closely at the book, you will see that Clark makes no mention of the spring, though it is quite clear that you have the same attitude towards me as Clark. So do you know that he doesn't mention the word "spring" anywhere?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, first of all, I did not mention General Clark's book yesterday. I said he published this remark in publications which he made in the United States of America. Secondly, I'm not aware of any attitude of General Clark towards you. I can only tell you that I have no specific attitude towards you. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even in his statement given to the journal "Parameters," a quarterly, he makes no mention of any spring. So my question is: Did you perhaps misquote my words, especially in view of the fact that such a cardinal statement was not used by you or Clark until 2001 by Clark and 2002 by you? Doesn't that seem too transparent to you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, again I may correct you. I believe that the fact of spring 1999 was mentioned by General Clark in one or the other of his publications; and secondly, I'm not using this statement as late as 2002. I have used this before, in discussions with people, in the public, when we discussed the Kosovo events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness's evidence was that during the talk you said -- this was his evidence, as I took it down: You said that you would try to find a solution of the Kosovo problem in spring 1999. Do you challenge that you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I challenge it. Of course I do. Isn't it quite logical, Mr. May, that just when we had signed an agreement, when everyone felt relieved, when we were talking about improving relations between ethnic communities, and everything else that I have quoted, that I should then say, "I won't observe any of that, but I'm going to execute them all in the spring"? Can anyone believe any such thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter what you say is logical, according to you. This is what the witness's evidence is that you said, that you would find a solution to the Kosovo problem in spring 1999. Since it's challenged, General, do you have any doubt that that was what was said by this accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I had had any doubts, I would not have stated this in front of this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, you didn't even tell the truth when you said what we drank. You said that we were drinking slivovitz. We were not drinking slivovitz, because I don't drink slivovitz. We were drinking pear brandy. So even regarding that detail, you were wrong, not to mention other things.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may forgive me that I'm not an expert on alcohol. Perhaps I confused that. But this does not mean that I did not tell the truth on other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Naumann. In view of the fact that reference is made to Drenica, the only parallel is with terrorism. It cannot refer to anything else but terrorism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been over this point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I'm showing you a document of the Prosecution, page 16, second paragraph, of the report by the historical expert of the Prosecution, Audrey Budding, which, although it is not objective or competent, nevertheless recognises that the partisans in the Drenica region --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I pointed out to you yesterday that as far as this witness's evidence is concerned, it doesn't matter what the history was. Whether you're telling the truth about it or not, it doesn't matter. The witness doesn't know what the history was, but it's what he said you said that matters. His evidence is that that is what you said. Now, whether it's a background for it or whether it's historically accurate, it doesn't matter. Now, there's no point going over it again with this witness. You've been over it several times.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Surely if there's a historical explanation, it becomes clear that I couldn't have said something that has nothing to do with the historical explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There may have been a hundred reasons why you've said it. It doesn't matter what the reasons are. It's the fact of your saying it which is of significance as far as this witness's evidence is concern. Now, we have exhausted this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Is it clear that the mention of Drenica has nothing to do with the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you're being asked how you interpreted the remark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, to the best of my recollection, there was no differentiation between bandits or civilian population. It was mentioned in a rather general way what Mr. Milosevic had in mind when he mentioned it, and I -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that. And secondly, are you claiming that I made no distinction between civilians and terrorists? Even the birds know that there was even an order that units of the army and the police may not open fire where civilians may be in danger. How, then, could someone say that no distinction was made between civilians and terrorists? Those orders exist, and they were complied with.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I not challenge, Mr. Milosevic, that such orders may have existed. The facts of the events which took place on the ground then indicate that some of your forces were not in compliance with the orders you had issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Naumann, that that very police and that very army, the army I had the honour to command, during the war arrested more than 500 persons who had committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that, Mr. Milosevic, but if they did so, well done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke to me about Racak. Is it clear -- is it true that I clearly told you that there was no massacre?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what you said. You rejected all our claims that the crime had committed -- had been committed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you had previously talked to Walker. In that conversation, did Walker tell you that Racak was a stronghold of the KLA where there was a KLA unit?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Walker told us during that conversation that initially there had been some KLA activity in that area and that your forces had taken action against that KLA area. And I referred to the fact yesterday that to the best of my knowledge, I think some seven KLA members had been killed by your forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Walker tell you -- I'm asking you about what Walker told you. The area is rather broad. I'm talking specifically about the village of Racak. Did he tell you that it was a KLA stronghold? Did Walker tell you that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did -- he did not call Racak a KLA stronghold. As I just stated a minute ago, Mr. Milosevic, he spoke about the fact that at Racak, some KLA activity had --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Could you please answer my questions with a yes and no, out of fairness, because my time is limited. Did he tell you that the fighting between the KLA and the police lasted from the morning until 4.00 p.m. in Racak?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may have been. I do not know whether he told us exactly the amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did he tell you that there was a report of his Verification Mission about the killed members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how, then, can you explain that in his statements he did not mention the killed members of the KLA but he only spoke of civilians in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Walker tell you that on that day, that critical day when the conflict between the police and the KLA took place in Racak, that OSCE observers were present? Did he inform you of that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentioned that the unarmed OSCE observers had been in the vicinity and that they withdrew as soon as the fighting started in order not to be in between the crossing lines of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's very good that you said that and quoted Walker to that effect.
