But linked to this Prosecution of crime within the territory of Yugoslavia that I mentioned an moment ago, how many people the army and the police had arrested as perpetrators of crimes, were you aware that in Serbia, already in 1992, several people were tried for war crimes committed in Bosnia, even before this institution was set up, before anyone spoke about it? As long ago as 1992, we tried individuals for war crimes committed in Bosnia. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, Mr. Milosevic, since it did never belong to my obligations to follow legal proceedings in your country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in that conversation when you referred to Racak, did I tell you explicitly that a conflict had occurred and that people had been killed in combat and that not a single Serb policeman would have committed such a crime?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, you said this, and I stated this in my evidence which is in written form in front of you. But I think we still have to make a difference between those KLA members which were killed in action and those -- I think there were 23 or so people who were not members of the KLA and who, according to the findings of the Finnish doctor, did not show the slightest signs of any involvement in combat operation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the findings of the Finnish, Belorussian, and Yugoslav pathologists do not differ, with the exception of one single case, to the effect that all had been killed by firearms fired from a distance and in movement? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, and I'm not aware of the fact that the findings of the Yugoslav and Belarus doctors do not -- do not differ from the findings of the Finnish. I am aware of the fact that the Finnish doctor stated that you and the Belarus doctors applied techniques which are outdated and not very accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was said in respect to the paraffin glove, which is a legal technique and which showed that 37 out of the 40 killed had used firearms to shoot with. And a paraffin glove --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, these are all matters which the Trial Chamber is going to have to determine. There's no point arguing with the witness about them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said, because of the lies conveyed to you by Walker, "I got very angry and started shouting." That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I repeat several times that the police and the army would never do something contrary to the law?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You stated that repeatedly, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did I then draw attention to the fact that I felt that Clark and Naumann, as well as Walker, had fallen into a trap by making such statements?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you said, and that is in my written evidence. And you know that we rejected that claim that we had fallen into a trap but that we simply had looked at the facts which were given to us by Ambassador Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did I inform you at the time that a Finnish team had been invited to do the abductions, post-mortems?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, and that's also part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I tell you that Walker had insulted the Yugoslav government?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also part of my statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was it logical for Yugoslav authorities, judicial, crime, and other institutions, to carry out the investigation? I mean the courts, the prosecution, the investigating magistrates, the crime department, the police, that they should do the abductions and pathological investigations on their territory when an instance of this kind occurs?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, when you're talking about logic, I wonder why you did not accept the offer which both Clark and I presented to you to invite Judge Arbour and her team to come to your countries. If you're talking about logic, nothing would be more logical than to have an objective, and that is a hypothetically impartial check of the events that took place. And the best instrument to that is an United Nations appointed Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of our position? Because you say that that was absolutely unbiased. But I am claiming that this court is an instrument of war against my country. Were you aware of our position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard all this. Now, what is the question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Talking about Louise Arbour, are you aware of our position that we considered this to be an illegal institution that was founded contrary to the United Nations Charter and that it was politically motivated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard all this several times. Now, let's go on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the indirect connection between Louise Arbour and terrorist KLA groups, as was evidenced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you're going to make these kind of allegations, you're going to have to support them. Now, you've got five minutes, five minutes more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why five? We started at five to -- five to eleven. If you gave me half an hour, then I have at least another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, make use of it sensibly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Do you know that Mrs. Arbour is a member of the board of management of the so-called international crisis group together with Thaci's advisor Abrahams and Wesley Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no point going on in this vein. If you have any other questions on any other topic so well and good. The witness has told you what he suggested, the fact that you rejected the suggestion. There seems to be little further point going on with it. You can produce your evidence in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a point to ask a witness when he doesn't know why I said that the political position of that group that I have listed the members of was bombing the independence of Kosovo and Montenegro, the abolition of Republika Srpska, the centralisation of Bosnia and so on. Is he aware of the positions of that group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, shall I answer to that question? It I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. There's no need to trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said in your statement that at the time, you gave me some ten examples of violations of the agreement; isn't that so? And that I took this from you and said that we would investigate it. Do you think that I could have said anything else, that I could have given you any other reply when faced with this from you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, in my view you could have given us another reply since many of the events which were on this list took place well before the 19th of January, but you preferred to say, "We'll look into that and we'll come back to you." The fact is that we never got an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you use the term "many," I remind you that you said that you gave information for some ten or so alleged violations of the agreement in total. So "many" can only mean a limited number. And do you know what kind of reports I received after looking into that information?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't know it since we never got an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Naumann, I was informed that you were not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you kindly elaborate on that? I can only tell you that I got never an answer. And I think the same is true for General Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I tell you, in respect to Solana's observation, that the Assembly of Serbia automatically approves Milosevic's decision that they, meaning the Assembly, has the last word? Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you told us and that's also part of my written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear that the ultimatum given to Yugoslavia was to accept an occupation that was contained in the Rambouillet agreement? Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- Mr. Milosevic, that is not true and you know that. I think that is part of really flawed information which you and others are promulgating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is the following true that I'm going to read out to you: [In English] "[Previous translation continues] ...appointed rulers of the planet issue an ultimatum to another country. It is surrender or die. To maintain our`credibility,'" that is under quotation, "`credibility', we must crush any semblance of resistance to our dictates to that country."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is saying that? Who are you quoting, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quoting Walter J. Rockler, former prosecutor of the Nuremberg war crimes trials. I'm quoting him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is simply the opinion of Mr. Rockler. No point putting it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, if there's no point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wish to ask the witness something in connection with his statement to the PBS Frontline, which I shall quote to refresh your memory [In English] "[Previous translation continues] ...which was fought for a principle, and the principle was that human rights have to be protected, and from that point of view, I think the Kosovo war is perhaps the first war in the European history which was fought for this principle, and by that we denied, we denied the continuing validity of the principle territorial integrity which dominated and still dominates international law since the Westphalian peace of 1648." [Interpretation] Does that mean that NATO decided to abolish the basic principle of international law, the principle of territorial integrity and sovereignty of states?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I referred to that earlier on. I think you quoted me correctly. And that's again part of the conviction at which I personally arrive, but others as well, that we have to find to -- a more modern understanding of what the sovereignty of states means. It cannot be seen exclusively as the right of a ruler to do to his citizens whatever he wishes to do, but it has to be seen as the responsibility of that ruler to protect human rights of his citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that those whose human rights you say were in jeopardy and they were terrorists and murderers, that they killed an enormous number of Albanians, and that the current leaders - and this was even shown and demonstrated even in this courtroom - committed murders of wealthy Albanians and others that they considered to be loyal to the authorities of Serbia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have repeatedly stated in public that I do not consider the KLA or UCK as an aggregation of angels, and that many of them misbehaved, grossly misbehaved. But you should not mix up the KLA activists who did not behave properly and the many thousands of innocent Kosovo Albanians who fell victim to the suppression executed by your security forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in my view, this is ground that we've already gone over. You're now repeating yourself. And in my view, your cross-examination is coming close to being abuse of the process of the Court. If you have no further questions that are germane to the issues, we should stop.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have questions, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that same interview that I quoted from a moment ago, in answer to a question whether you consider such humanitarian intervention to be justified, you declared that in political practice you doubt their justification because of cases such as the hesitation of the international community in Eastern Timor and looking the other way when the Russians were violating human rights in Chechnya; is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Milosevic, but the hesitation of the international community does not rule out that on one occasion the international community acted in legitimacy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question. This must be your last question. It's now 11.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you agree with the former German defence minister, Rupert Schultz, who said -- who spoke at a meeting of the Bundeswehr, and I quote: [In English] "We are concerned with dealing with the consequences of World War I." He was referring to the destruction of Yugoslavia when he said: "Yugoslavia, being a consequence of World War I, is a very artificial construct which has never been compatible with the idea of self-determination." [Interpretation] Is that in the background of such selective interpretations of policies and pressures under which Yugoslavia was broken up? Is that the ideology? Is it the same ideology as from the First and Second World Wars?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I am not here to comment on statements of German politicians. I can only assure you that these historical connotations did not play a role when NATO took its decision. The decision was based on severe violations of human rights and on the necessity to restore the stability of an entire region which was endangered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you claiming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No more questions. Mr. Tapuskovic, have you any questions you wish to ask the witness? Although time is rather limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In view of the sensitivity of the moment, I should like to ask you how much time I can reckon with, so that I can make a selection of my questions, and I will do my best to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The general has to leave by midday. Twenty minutes, Mr. Tapuskovic, should be more than enough. We've been cross-examining for two hours or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope it will be enough, yes. Thank you, Your Honours. In order to assist the Court -- this is not a question for the general, but in order to assist you, Your Honours, I should like to draw your attention to the fact that in view of the questions that were asked yesterday, in the draft of the expert finding of Budding, on page 16, you have sufficient data from which you are able to see what happened in Drenica between 1945 and 1949. And I just wanted to draw your attention to that. You have the information there, how many Yugoslav soldiers were engaged there in a war that lasted four years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, as I've said quite plainly, it doesn't matter what happened in Drenica it's in 1940s, as far as this evidence is concerned. The witness has said this is what the accused told him. Now, that's an end of it. Whatever happened in Drenica is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't wish to ask the general this. I just wanted to assist the Trial Chamber and draw your attention to those facts in that report which you have

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the first question I have for the general is the following, and it has to do with one particular matter. You said that you had decided to do what you did in the interests that you stipulated, the UN General Assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not speak of the UN General Assembly. I think when you refer to the justification for the intervention --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Security Council, I meant.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the Security Council on one occasion. I said that the Security Council in the Kosovo crisis was not able to do its duty since it did not achieve agreement, and in that exceptional situation, the NATO nations decided to take actions which they believed was legitimate, although the authorisation by the Security Council was lacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm interested in something else. Perhaps that might be more important. Did the parliaments of all the countries, the member states of NATO, did all those parliaments, the parliaments of all those countries, approve that action of yours; and if not, which of them did not? Did, for instance, the parliament of your country approve the action?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The German parliament approved the participation of German armed forces in this operation, with a majority which would be sufficient to alter the German constitution. With regard to the other countries, all those countries where there is a necessity, a legal necessity to ask for parliamentary approval of such operations, approved the operation. But it's not necessary in all NATO countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did all the parliaments approve?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I just said, it's not necessary in all NATO countries that the parliaments approve. It depends on the national legislation, which differs from country to country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you know that when this decision was taken by NATO, the activation order that you yourself mentioned, that via the Yugoslav Albanian border, for a considerable period of time, arms were carried illegally, in substantial quantities, and brought into the territory of Kosovo. You've already said that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We saw that smuggling took place, and as I said, we tried to take action to stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that before the 15th of October, on the territory of Kosovo, that armed groups of Albanians existed, and they carried out a number of violent actions against the army and the police, and I think that is proper what you said. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But again, I should remind you that one should not look at this in isolation. The armed resistance of Kosovar Albanians against Yugoslav suppression is also the result of actions which took place long before the armed resistance began.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, my question is the following: Does that mean that in addition to the existence of this constant illegal smuggling and introduction of weapons to Kosovo, and the facts as to the violence on the part of the armed Albanians - I'm not saying whether they're terrorists or rebels or whatever but that they were armed - what that justified that you should ask from that state in which this was happening to reduce the number of soldiers and policemen to the number that was there in peacetime, despite these two facts? So were these peace conditions, the same conditions that existed as they did in peacetime? And that was the condition made, that these numbers should be reduced to what they were in peacetime. Now, tell me, please: Were these peacetime conditions?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you may remember, in summer 1998, the Yugoslav security forces undertook really quite extensive operations to crush the KLA and the armed resistance. And what we intended to achieve is a return to normalcy which would allow both sides to return to a peaceful living together, as it, by the way, is clearly expressed in this statement which we signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in view of the fact that the conditions were not peaceful ones, the position that you took in the negotiations and that you expounded yesterday, could it have been -- could you have used the argumentation you used, that is to say that you came and said that you had authority to attack unless the conditions stipulated were complied with?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we wanted to achieve conditions under which a cessation of hostilities could take place, and one precondition to that was to reduce the number of forces in the country and to limit the disproportionate response to incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me this, General: Had the army withdrew, to your surprise, and the police, and had this taken you by surprise, and had they withdrawn from these areas and regions, but had the KLA taken control of these regions, could that have been a reason for that police force and that state to gain back control of the territory that had been left in order to achieve these peaceful conditions?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not entirely so that the KLA more or less filled the vacuum completely. They tried, on one or the other occasion, and in other incidents it was action taken by the security forces which triggered the incidents. I think I have explained that repeatedly in my statements yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No. What I'm saying is when the army actually withdrew, this area was taken over by the others. That's what I'm talking about. Once the police had withdrawn, the KLA took control of these areas, and the police and army withdrew in order to abide by these peaceful circumstances and conditions. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tapuskovic, as far as I know, this is not entirely the case, not 100 per cent. This happened occasionally. And in other areas nothing happened; it remained as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, the NATO council, did it know about the estimated number of armed Albanians who performed and perpetrated the acts that you talked about? Did you have information of that kind?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had some information. Whether we had the full information or not, I simply dare not to say, since, as you know, intelligence is always based on the availability of sources, and we definitely did not have 100 per cent information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the Verification Mission had begun its work. Now, I'm interested in the following: During your first conversation, and then with respect to your second conversation, and especially when, on the 19th of January, you talked again, were there any facts and figures or information as to the number? A high-ranking official, officer, Mr. Ciaglinski, of the Verification Mission, said that there was knowledge about 10.000 KLA members at a given moment. Now, did you have the same information that the OSCE had at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OSCE shared its information with us, and I can only tell Your Honours that the figures varied again and again, and we never had a clear-cut, agreed-by-everyone figure which indicated the full strengths of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, here's why I'm asking you this, General. As you are an officer, and as you are well acquainted with military doctrine - I'm a layman in that area myself - can you agree with the following observation, bearing in mind military doctrine: What could the ratio of state forces be against armed people in any state, in any country? What ratio would this be? We keep speaking about what is proportionate and what is disproportionate. What would a ratio be? Now, I have read some things. Would the ratio be, say, 3:1? And it even goes as high as 6:1, that ratio. That is to say the state, a state, can, under certain circumstances, use three men, three of its men, against one armed individual, whether terrorist or otherwise. Do you have any knowledge as to that, linked to military doctrine, and how important that was for your assessments?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, this is not a question of military doctrine, since we are talking about internal security, and that's normally the responsibility of police forces. But in order to arrive at a balanced judgement of what the strengths of police forces should be, we did some comparative calculations in NATO to compare, I should say, the police density in Kosovo under peacetime conditions, the 10.024 individuals Mr. Milosevic mentioned, to other areas, where we have, let's say, a high rate of criminality, and we came to the conclusion that the 10.000-or-so figure is approximately commensurate to the security challenges in this part of former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would -- that would be that. Now, I would like to move on to Racak, the topic of Racak. Ambassador Walker, before the meeting with Milosevic on the 19th of January, informed you of the events in Racak. He presented the view and the position that the victims were civilians and gave his reasons for doing so, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you accepted that evaluation of his, that assessment?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had the unique advantage, compared to the two of us, General Clark and myself, that he had been on the site and that he had seen what had happened, at least with regard to the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page -- that is to say, in paragraph 31 of your statement, in your last sentence, you said that they also told him that one of the victims was a 14-year-old boy. Did Walker tell you that or somebody else, or was it Walker who told you that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Mr. Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come to learn whether this was true among the people who were in the ditch? Was there, in fact, a 14-year-old boy among them? Did you ever learn whether that was true or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw other publications which indicated that there was a youngster among them. Whether he was 14 years old or perhaps 13 or 12, I don't know. But it was indicated that there were among these I think 23 people women, as well as one youngster.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that was later on. I'm interested in what you came to learn before the 19th of January, before you were to meet with Mr. Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There the main evidence was the information we got from Ambassador Walker, and he also told us that there were women among them and there was a boy, a young boy, among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said - we won't repeat it, but could you please confirm it - that there were also victims; that is to say, some members of the KLA were also killed. Right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was also a piece of information which Ambassador Walker shared with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm interested in this: Did anybody tell you that - it was exactly on the 15th of January, before you were to meet Mr. Milosevic - did anybody tell you then that on the 15th of January, in that circle, that two policemen were killed as well?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was mentioned also by Mr. Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Walker tell you, or anybody else, did they tell you that on the 18th of January, that is to say, the day when the bodies were taken over, the bodies which the Serb investigating authorities wished to take for their expert findings, that according to the OSCE reports on those days, 17 Serb policemen were killed in front of the mosque in which those bodies were placed? Did you know about that when you went to talk to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that Mr. Walker mentioned that there had been an incident, but I do not recall the number of police officers being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't know about the 17 policemen killed. So you were told about the two policemen who were killed on the 15th. You were also told about the 17 policemen killed in front of the mosque. Did anybody tell you that one day prior to that, that is to say, on the 18th, in the period between the 15th and the 19th, when you were to see Slobodan Milosevic, that a further number of Serb policemen had been killed and that the total number killed between the 15th and 19th was 47 policemen? Did you know that at the time or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know the figure of 47 police officers, and I'm not aware -- and I do not know whether this was taking place in the area of Racak or whether the 47 are related to incidents elsewhere in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we conclude that prior to your conversation with Slobodan Milosevic, that you did not know what the injuries and wounds to the victims from Racak were except for what Walker told you? And that's what you said yesterday, that they were all hit in the neck, or that most of them were hit in the neck.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to emphasise what you last said, that most of them were hit in the neck. He told us that, and he showed us, I think, one or two photographs which he had taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But General, all those forensic findings have been dovetailed, and we are faced with a situation in which there are no further dilemmas on that score. Now, the injuries, the wounds, were predominantly in the chest and the head, in the region of the chest and head --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we've been over this, you know, a great deal. It's not helpful to go over it again. The witness can only deal with what he was told at the time. It's for us to determine what happened and to look at all the forensic results. It's not helpful for further examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know that, Your Honours. I'm aware of that. But the General said yesterday that if the injuries are gained in combat, that they are usually injuries to the chest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We know. We know. And you're going to say, "But they weren't in the neck." Very well. You can make the point. It's no good arguing with the witness about it. He just made a point on what he was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no need to argue, and I will skip over that question. But may I now address the issue of deportation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you would be fairly brief, because the witness has a plane to catch and he must leave by 12.00, and it's right there should be some re-examination, and you've been nearly 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have to ask him about deportation and NATO bombing and that will complete my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said the operation, the deportation operation and the expulsion was very well planned and that it began after the NATO bombing. That's what you said. Now, my question to you is the following: Were the plans for exportation of the Albanian population outside the territory of Kosovo, could they have been made if NATO bombing was not a known fact? Because the people did start leaving at the very point when the NATO bombing started.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tapuskovic, there is something which I think you misquoted when you referred to me. I stated yesterday that based on the information we had got, the expulsion, if I may say so, of Kosovo Albanians started before NATO had bombed, and it was then accelerated. So I think we have to correct your impression in that respect and bring it back to the line which I took yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the members of the Verification Mission? Did they leave Kosovo first and foremost because the NATO bombing was due to start and so they left for their own security and safety, or was it what you said yesterday, so that they would not remain as hostages and become hostages?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were concerned about the security of the OSCE observers and invited the OSCE to consider NATO's recommendation to withdraw them since we saw that the bombing was imminent. And the OSCE then took the decision to withdraw them, I think on the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We have been speaking over these days and months that the Albanians were fleeing Kosovo for certain reasons. I don't want to go back to that now. Do you have any information as to the number, how many from the territory of Serbia and the rest of Serbia, so Serbia proper, Vojvodina, et cetera, how many Hungarians from Subotica went to Hungary, how many Serbs fled to Serb Krajina, how many Romanians escaped to Romania, and in general terms how many people from Belgrade, for instance, who had the ability -- the possibility of leaving Serbia left because of the danger of NATO bombing? Did you have any information as to the problems these neighbouring states had because of the people from Serbia who were leaving en masse, who were fleeing from their country en masse? Did you have any information of that kind? Because half of Budapest was, for example, was inhabited by Serbs who had fled. Or didn't you have information of that kind?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information that people left their homes, also people of another nationalities, and that this number, of course, increased when the air operation started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And just one -- several more points with respect to the NATO bombing. You say in your statement, in paragraph 39 to be exact, towards the end, with respect to the NATO report from the meeting, and it says Naumann's decoded notes from the meeting, and then under an asterisk here it says: "One should be clear if we undertake military action, we will end up in the field, in the terrain." Does that mean when you undertook this action you had decided to go on the ground, action then end up on the ground, that you decided to use ground troops, the infantry, and go on the ground? That's what it says. "Need to be clear: should we take mil action then end up on the ground." That's what you said in your statement.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tapuskovic, that was my statement, that was my assessment, and that was my statement to the NATO council telling them that if they take the decision to intervene by air operations, that they, at the end of the day, may end up with a necessity to include and involve ground forces. I wanted to make them aware of the necessity to be prepared to see it through, since you should never start an intervention if you're not prepared to escalate as appropriate and also if you're not prepared to stay in the country in which you acted in order to restore peace and stability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you've had -- you've had nearly half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One more question and then we must give a chance for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two more questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Tapuskovic, please don't argue. We cannot go on in this way. This is ground which is all covered. And speaking for myself, I do not find it helpful for the amicus to be taking these sort of points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, this is the point of what I wish to ask: What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What quantity of uranium bombs were called when the operation was called Angel -- what quantity of these types of these bombs were thrown on Kosovo? And in the military sense, did you think that it was all okay for bombs to be thrown from a height of 10.000 metres? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tapuskovic, I cannot give you detailed numbers and figures on the amount of depleted uranium that was used. With regard to the height, the 15.000 feet flight level, there are two elements which you should consider. First is, of course, to some extent we decided to take this flight level in order to protect the pilots against air defence missiles. And one other not too often discussed issue is that if you use laser-guided ammunition, the 15.000 feet flight level is presumably the optimum flight level to allow the biggest accuracy of the laser-guided ammunition. So that was another step which I think was taken in order to ensure that the utmost care was taken to ensure accuracy of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld. I'm afraid there's just five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand that, and accordingly, I will reduce my re-examination and restrict it to one area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: General Naumann, both yesterday and today, you were challenged on whether or not the accused, in fact, made the statement that you claim he made on the 25th of October concerning the Drenica incident. It was suggested to you, sir, that you fabricated that statement. I believe in response you indicated that you were aware that those statements were made previously, not only by you but by General Clark, is that correct, and that you had read publications?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This morning it was put to you that -- there was a quote from a book. You said you weren't referring to the book. Are you aware that such a book exists by General Clark?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that General Clark has written a book on Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that book? Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not read it in detail. General Clark kindly gave it to me and I read the concluding part in detail, but I did not read all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have for Your Honours' benefit a copy of a few pages of that book I'd like to put to the witness. It is entitled -- there are only four pages. The first page is a cover page called "Waging Modern War," by General Wesley Clark. The second page is the date of publication or copyright, 2001. And then there's an excerpt from pages 151 and 152. And just so that everybody is clear, this is part of a disclosure package that was given -- it's on our witness -- it's on our exhibit list under K2591, and I'm referring to pages K2 -- 0209078 through to pages K0209101.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very briefly, General. At the bottom of page 151, there is reference, third to the last paragraph, which starts with the words: "And so the paper was completed ...," et cetera, et cetera. And then the next paragraph refers to Milosevic bringing in "... brandy in for himself, Milutinovic and me, and for once I joined him. He grew philosophical... began to discuss the economic future of Serbia." And then he - I'm skipping - he abruptly changed subjects and he said, and I propose to quote: "`You know, General Clark, that we know how to handing these Albanians, these murderers, these rapists, these killers-of-their-own-kind. We've taken care of them before.' His face turned red, and his voice rose in strength as he condemned them. This is the paragraph out of some public statement. He wasn't really speaking to us, I thought. "`In Drenica in 1946, we killed them all. We killed them all.' Naumann and I were just staring at him. "He must have thought we didn't believe him, so he began to qualify the accomplishment. `Oh, it took several years but we eventually killed them all.'" How, if at all, does that accord with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is not -- not too far away from what I stated, and it confirms what I had said. The wording is slightly different but all in all I think it's identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Similarly, sir, you indicated that there was another publication to which you originally referred, and you said it was not the book yesterday. Were you referring to an interview on Frontline by any chance?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could well be. But, Mr. Ryneveld, forgive me if I don't know exactly the publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But you were aware of other publications?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very briefly, sir, I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honours, I could show another document. Again this has been the subject of disclosure. It's exhibit list reference OTP number K2328. It is -- purports to be a copy of an interview with General Clark, and at the bottom it says -- it's a "Frontline War in Europe Interview" with General Wesley Clark on the 14th of November, 2001. In response to various questions on page 6 of 19 pages -- and I'll wait until Your Honours have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You want these exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Oh, yes, please. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: First document Prosecution Exhibit 231. Last document 232.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Again, sir, do you see the third paragraph from the top of page 6 starting with three dots just before that rectangle? There's a five-line paragraph which refers to: "He recounted to us that he knew how to deal with the Albanians, that in 1946, the Albanians that he called `murderers and bandits,' were handled by `killing them all, although it took several years, we killed them all.' He then signed the promises to NATO that he would use only normal policing methods." Is that the publication or a publication like it to which you referred to in evidence?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS NAUMANN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a publication like it, Mr. Ryneveld. I'm not sure whether it was this one or another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that be given an exhibit number? And those are all my questions in light of the time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This was already exhibited. 232.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I had my headphones off. Were we just given a number? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we usually take the break at ten past twelve.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We do, Your Honours, and I propose for the balance of the time after the break to call the first of two crime base witnesses, depending on the time. I will, however, anticipate that at some point today I'd like to address you on a couple of issues, administrative issues. I'm asking when that might be the most convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why not now?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you. I was hoping you'd say that. The first matter, Your Honours, has to do with the discussion that Mr. Nice had with the Court concerning a decision on the Rule 70 issue, and reference was made to a matter that we believed at that time to be a 22 confidential decision. It in fact is a public decision. And in that decision decision, the Ambassador was referred to under a pseudonym, and the (redacted)is mentioned as a government. I just wanted you to be aware that we will be providing a copy of that since it is a public decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you would do that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We shall. The other thing, Your Honours, is that there is before the Court at the moment an application by the Prosecution to consider, to use the expression, to fully bis, in other words, allow a 92 bis statement in without cross-examination for some witnesses, one of which is K24, and the other one is K31. My understanding is that filling and scheduling arrangements are extremely difficult and there is a schedule that they would be flying in next week. So I'm simply asking if the Court might turn its attention to that in sufficient time for us to alter scheduling in the event the Court is in accord with our request. And finally -- excuse me just one moment while I get a clarification of a note.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The final matter, Your Honours, is the issue of perhaps when Mr. Nice might address you with respect to some further administrative matters. I understand that the Court may be disposed to hear us on Tuesday. However, there is one issue that have will have been dealt with earlier and that involves the witness that was the subject of discussions in private session, and we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can tell you we're not in a position to deal with that. We were told the witness can wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we -- it's a matter which is going to take very serious consideration, and we are not in a position to deal with it at the beginning of next week. We will try and deal with it in the middle of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So the request that I've been handed is would it be possible by Tuesday afternoon. I take it from your answer that is unlikely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think I have to tell you it's unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are the administrative matters that I wanted to deal with, and after the break, I propose to call the first of our two witnesses, Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard the application in regard to K24, and K31. They both deal with the same sort of subject matter, and perhaps you could reflect over the weekend whether you wish to cross-examine them or not, and it's a matter that we can deal with on Monday. There's no need to say anything at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you straight away I insist on cross-examining them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider that matter. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, I wonder if you could tell the Court your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Thaqi Milazim, Hetimi, from the village the Broje, municipality of Skenderaj in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how old, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I am 53 -- correction, 56 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly, sir, that you you were married in 1970 and you have nine children of the marriage?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And I understand that five of those children are still living with you at home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: At least in March of 1999, five of them were living with you at home?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Thaqi, you've told us that you are from Broje. Do I understand correctly, sir, at some point you --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- you found yourself in the village of Izbica on the 28th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a moment. Did you --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to investigators of the Tribunal on the 9th and 12th of November of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you give a further statement for clarification on the 17th and 20th the of October of the year 2001?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I gave that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Recently, sir, on the 10th of June of 2002, did you have an opportunity to review those statements you gave and appear before an officer of this Tribunal and indicate under solemn declaration --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- that those statements were true to the best of your knowledge, information, and belief?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps those statements might now be distributed and marked as an exhibit. And while that's being done, I propose, if I may, to simply read a brief summary of what is contained in that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 233.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding is that the witness's statement is that Serb troops came close to his village of Broje on the 25th of March, 1999, where there was a KLA presence. He and his family left their home in Broje on the 26th of March and went to the village of Izbica, about five or six kilometres distant. Now, Izbica was considered to be a safer place because there was no known KLA presence in that village, according to the witness. The rest of the population of Broje also left for Izbica in a large convoy of assorted vehicles, and of course some on foot. They gathered together with a large number of refugees in a field outside of Izbica. He estimates that several thousand people were in this area from all over Skenderaj municipality. You will note that in his statement he describes that on the morning of the 28th of March, 1999, which happened to be the Muslim holy day of Bajram, at about 9.30 in the morning, that field was surrounded by Serb troops, which consisted of a mixture of both army and police forces, and in his statement he describes the different uniforms worn by the Serb forces. He tells you that the soldiers demanded money from the crowd and that he saw many people handing over large amounts of money. The witness personally handed over 30 Deutschmarks. After a while, men were separated from the women and children and were ordered to sit in four rows on the road. The majority of the men were elderly. He estimates that there were about 150 men in total. The witness then goes on to describe in his statement that the men were physically and verbally abused. They heard someone, whom he believed to be the commander in charge, say to the policemen, "Everybody knows their duty. Now, do it." The men were divided and taken away in two groups, in opposite directions. The witness was in one of those groups of about 33 men who were taken in two lines towards the woods, escorted by one policeman armed with a machine-gun. After some 200 to 250 metres or so, they were stopped close to a water channel. They were still in two lines and were ordered to kneel down facing the woods. The policeman then opened fire from about eight metres' distance. No other police were seen by the witness to be nearby. There was a continuous burst of machine-gun fire. Two persons fell against the witness and knocked him to the ground. One was his cousin, Uke Uka, who was aged 74 years. He describes the injuries of that witness and that he was hit by debris. The witness himself was not hit, but laid still until the shooting was over. He estimates that the shooting lasted only a matter of seconds, and he then heard a single shot. He later discovered that bullets had penetrated his jacket, his jersey, and his shirt, without harming him. They appeared to have come from the side, skimming over his back. The witness then describes some of the perpetrators in his statement. Well, after the shooting was over, the witness remained quiet and unmoving on the ground for about half an hour, he says. During this time, he heard more automatic gunfire. It was the other men being killed. Then, hearing what he thought were tanks returning, he, with two other survivors, Sheqir Halil and Jetish Qallapeki, moved into the woods. He and Sheqir remained in the woods until around 7.00 p.m., and then they walked into the neighbouring village of Vojnike. He said he came back to Izbica on the 1st of April, 1999 and participated in the burial of bodies. And he describes there were 147 victims but some had been taken by their families and buried elsewhere. A hundred and thirty of those were buried in Izbica. He also indicates that when he returned to his home in Broje on the 14th of June, 1999, he found his house burned, his property destroyed, and some of his livestock and farm animals missing. And I ought to have done this at the outset, Your Honours, but if you can look at what has been marked as the Kosovo atlas 2, I might refer Your Honours to page 5, and at the top you'll see an "L," and then down the right-hand column you'll see "13." If you see where they match, just down to the bottom you'll see Izbica, and that's just above line 30, the horizontal line. And then if you go about an inch down, into the next square, you'll see Broje. That, I understand, is the village of Broje from which the witness originated, and that's about five to six kilometres from Izbica, according to his statement, if that assists the Court in noting where it is. Now, I propose to show the witness, Mr. -- or Madam Usher, and ask you, if you would, please, to show this to the witness, and after he's had a chance to look at it, put it on the ELMO. And Your Honours, this is an aerial photograph of Izbica, which you can find in your binders, Izbica binder, tab 2 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, would you just look at the photograph, the aerial photograph. I don't know if you can see it well enough on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, I cannot distinguish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There we go. There are some --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There are some letters on the screen. First of all, there's a letter "A," which is now off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There is a letter "A." Do you see that? And it points to --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Letter "A" indicates the places where there were victims. We were the first group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And in your statement you've described the first group being taken somewhere. Is the place where you were taken and shot at, is that shown --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- anywhere in this photo?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I cannot really see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might I ask you, Witness, to turn to your left and look at the actual photograph that's lying on the ELMO. It will be easier for you to see.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you see number "B"?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: "B," here. We were here, the first group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what happened there, at where the arrow from "B" points to? What happened at that location?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: When they sent us there, they told us to stop, and told us to stop near a wall, at a distance of eight metres. They told us to turn our backs towards them, and so we did. We were told to kneel. And before we actually kneeled, they opened automatic fire on us, and I fell down on the ground. I had a victim close to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: After that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, I've already summarised your statement. I just want to be able to assist the Court in orienting where these things happened. So "B" is the place where you were shot, is that correct, where the group of you were shot at?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you see a letter "C"? Look at the diagram --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- on your left. Yes. Do you see a letter "C"? I don't --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what does the letter "C" -- how does that assist the Court? What happened there, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That's where the second group was. I don't know how many victims were of that group there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You're aware that a second group of people were killed, and that's in that area, "C"?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Moving to the letter "D" --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll have to move that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: "D" is where the third group was. I don't know how many people they killed of that group. They were close to the woods. And of the second and third group, there were no survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And we're having some difficulty seeing it on the ELMO. And finally, at letter "E," if we can find that ---

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I don't see it being displayed on the ELMO, but... Top left-hand corner. Yes. Do you see the letter "E," sir, on the top left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What does that describe?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This is where the fourth group was, on the right-hand side. Many were killed there. Nine of them were saved, survived. They survived the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, I'd like to show you a series of three photographs, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Madam Usher, if we can remove that, and I'll give you three photographs. And Your Honours, you will find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me have that photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The next three photographs, Your Honour, is in the Izbica binder, at tab 2, and they're photos 2, 3, and 4 in that binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The first one, sir, seems to show an item of apparel, a garment. Do you recognise that item shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This is my shirt, the shirt in which the bullet came through.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can you point to the bullet holes?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. Here is one, here, and here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Next photograph. What's that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This is my jumper, which also has three bullet holes in the back. One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the next photograph. What's that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: This is my jacket. It also has one, two, and I cannot see the third one, but I know that there were three bullet holes in this one too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those bullet holes, sir, is it your evidence that those bullet holes were as a result of the shooting incident, or were they there before?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: These -- that day. This is what happened that day. When I fell down on the ground, the bullets hit me in my back, on my clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Finally, sir, I'm going to show you a fold-out photograph that is a still photo of a video, and it's got -- first of all, do you recognise the scene of the bodies in that photograph? Have you seen that photograph before?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is that a photograph of the people -- the group that you were with who were shot?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can you indicate to the Court on that photograph, to the best of your recollection, where you were in relation to that pile of bodies --

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I was here, in the middle of the bodies. I was here. And then here was Uke and Isuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those are my questions of the witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the photograph comes back, please. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, on the 25th of March, 1999, after the beginning of the NATO air raid, the police set up checkpoints at Josanica, at about three kilometres from Broje. That's what you stated in your statement. What did NATO bomb in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. NATO did not bomb in our area at all, nowhere in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before that date that you mention, you left the village on two occasions - in March 1998 and in July 1998 - is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the real reason for you to leave? Was it perhaps the fact that at the time, as in March 1999, there was fighting between the KLA and the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb forces attacked us, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many were there on the other side, the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I do not know how many of them there were, but there was KLA presence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction. Was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me simply -- oh, there were none. I see.

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not get at cross-purposes. It's important to distinguish. Were the KLA in the village before March 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was. However, there were more in other areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And was there any fighting on the 28th of March -- or rather - I'm sorry - earlier, when you left the village. Was there fighting that day or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, not that day. There was no fighting that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was there fighting between the police and the army and the KLA, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: When there was fighting? I don't know exactly when, but there was some fighting around Jashareva. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was in reference to the time before this day that you mention, that you left the village on two occasions: in March 1998 and July 1998. In those days, in March and July 1998, was there any fighting in those days between the KLA and the police and army?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I left, and I don't know whether there was fighting or not, but certainly there must have been fighting going on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you leave the village in July 1998 and in March 1998? Why did you leave the village in March 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Why we left? We left because the Serbian army came from the municipality of Klina on the 5th of March. They came, so we left. And on the 30th of July, they came again, from both sides - from the asphalt road and from Resnik - so we left, in order to go somewhere to hide, in order not to fall in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Either in March or in July, were they looking for somebody? Did they open fire at somebody? Did they shoot at somebody? Or were they just passing through?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No. They killed that day two or three people, and then they set off towards somewhere. They left Broje, and I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were those two or three people that they killed that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I don't know their names. They were from different villages around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were from different villages and they were there. Were they in uniform or were they in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No. They were all in civilian. They were young, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No. No. What weapons? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was precisely in your area that there were many KLA forces - the 145th Brigade of the KLA was there - and that in the whole region about two and a half thousand, the 111th, 112th, 113th, 114th, 140th in your area? Do you know all that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I know that there were some. How many there were, that I do not know. But I do know that there were some of them, and they were in Jashanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And according to my information, there were about two and a half thousand of them. Were there that many or were there less?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That I do not know. These things are not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that you were afraid of what the Serbs might do when, you said, the police set up checkpoints three kilometres away from your village. Why were you afraid of a police checkpoint that was three kilometres away from your village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Because we saw even before in Recak, we saw in Likoshan, in Cirez, and that's why we were scared. We saw what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Ryneveld was reading a summary of your statement, you said that you went to Izbica because there was no KLA there, so you considered it to be safer. Isn't that right? You went to Izbica because there was no KLA there, and you thought it was safer there because the KLA was not there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I stated, because that's what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in your village, that means that there were KLA there, and that's why you left it and went to Izbica, where there were no KLA members. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: There was no KLA in our village that day. Not that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what day was the KLA there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: What day? I don't know what day. But that day there was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But since you went to Izbica, the reason for your going to Izbica was that there were no KLA there. Why did you leave your village if there were no KLA in your village?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Because they came from the municipality of Klina and they started Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. shooting with their weapons, so we left. We heard the shots and we left. We left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the fact that you went to this place Izbica was because there were no KLA there. Does that mean that where the KLA were present, it was dangerous because of possible clashes between the KLA and the police?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: In Izbica village there was no KLA that day. Where there was KLA, the Serbian army did not dare go in, except - correction - they only entered in areas where there were elderly people, women, and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who went to the area where there were elderly people, women, and children? Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The Serbian army, your army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it didn't go where the KLA were?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, does that mean, then, that the police and the army did not fight the KLA anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No. We did fight. But I don't know. I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. As the army and the police was not in contact with the KLA in your area, how do you explain the great number of soldiers who were killed in your area? Who killed these soldiers, then?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The Serbian army. Who else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the large number of persons killed - that is to say, our soldiers, soldiers belonging to the army of Yugoslavia - in that particular area. Who killed them, if you say that there were only civilians there?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know whether there were victims from the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, on the 1st of April, 1999, precisely in your village -- I have a figure here. My information tells me that a soldier was killed, or rather, a member of the MUP, in your particular village. His name was Igor Vrosevic. He was killed. And then in Likovac, for example, several of them there, and several in Mrkalj, more in Likovac again, and so on, also a large number of soldiers in that whole area of yours, in the Srbica municipality. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't hear of any fighting in which the army and police and the KLA members lost their lives in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: I have not heard about that. I was trying to leave with my family to seek shelter somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say in your statement that on the night of the 26th of March, "... my friends from Izbica, Gani Rama received my family to spend the night in one of the rooms of his house. And during that particular night, it was very difficult to sleep because of the constant shelling." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That's right. That's what it was. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what kind of constant shelling was this? Was it bombing? What was it that was so loud that you couldn't sleep the whole night?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: That is where those came from, the Serbian army. From your army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And which village was shelled on the 27th of March? You say that it was shelled by our army. Which villages were in fact shelled?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Turiqevc, Kobiliq, Jashareva. These villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you and your family, from the 26th of March to the 28th of March, in the morning, did you have any problems while you stayed at Gani Rama's place?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any problem whatsoever. He received us very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is Hashim Thaqi a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: [In Serbian] Yes, he is. [In Albanian] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it a member of the same family? So he's a member of your family?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, who told you that there were 157 of you? Did you count this or did somebody tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILAZIM THAQI
utterances.text: The victims?
